newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: FOCUS-OPEC ministers predict a quota rollover.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-OPEC ministers predict a quota rollover.

text.p: OPEC oil ministers said at Vienna talks on Thursday they expect to wrap up an accord to freeze their output quotas, a measure they hope will keep petroleum prices high despite Iraq's likely resumption of exports.

Several ministers predicted a "roll over" of the current production accord, which already includes provision for extra Iraqi oil, at the session of the Organisation of the Petroleum Exporting Countries.
"Everybody is talking about a rollover" said Kuwait's minister, Isa al-Mazeedi. "Should there be a rollover it is fair to expect it to go for six months".
OPEC conferred in Vienna after the U.N. Security Council made new progress toward easing its Gulf War ban on Iraq.
A council committee on Wednesday approved a pricing formula to remove one of the final hurdles to an oil-for-food deal with the Iraqis.
Iraq's chief OPEC delegate, Osama al-Hiti, said in Vienna he expected to resume oil sales within "a matter of weeks".
"If the tanker comes tomorrow we can fill it up", he said.

Baghdad hosted a 1960 meeting that created OPEC but hasn't been allowed to sell oil since it invaded fellow founder member Kuwait in 1990. The U.N. accord would let it sell $2 billion worth to buy food and medicine.

For its part, OPEC is enjoying a bonanza of strong oil prices partly because of delays in implementing the U.N. deal since President Saddam Hussein sent troops to northern Iraq during Kurdish faction fighting in September.
As oil firms scurried to replenish the West's depleted stocks of winter heating fuel, the benchmark Brent Blend of crude ended Wednesday at almost $22.75 per barrel.
That compares with only $18 when OPEC last met, in June, and the oil ministers were not about to make any rash moves as they entered Thursday's session of talks.
Delegates say cartel linchpin Saudi Arabia favours a freeze on current quotas at least to the end of June.

Iran's Gholamreza Aqazadeh has said he would support a 12-month freeze, although others thought that the consensus was for six months. Indonesia, OPEC's only Asian member, joined the consensus. Ministers said they may wrap up a deal on Thursday.

"OPEC is meeting against a backdrop that can only bring a smile to their lips", said Peter Gignoux, head of the London energy desk at brokers Smith Barney. "Oil is up five dollars. That is in itself an incentive to preserve the status quo".
Prices are strong despite both the prospect that the ban on Iraqi exports will be relaxed and OPEC's own quota violations.
Al-Hiti says only "very minor technicalities" now need to be ironed out before Iraq can export 700,000 to 800,000 barrels daily using up in full his OPEC quota allocation.
The ghost at the OPEC feast was that quota violations have already lifted actual output almost a million barrels per day above its agreed ceiling of 25.03 million, even before Iraq sells any oil.
Venezuela alone is alleged to be busting its mandatory quota by as much as Iraq is likely to sell.
Iran's Aqazadeh aired that matter in a bilateral session on Wednesday with Erwin Arrieta of Venezuela. He said the Venezuelan denied being over quota by a single barrel.
Saudi Arabia is said by a Gulf source to believe that the market is robust enough to absorb more oil.
